title: The can opener came 50 years late
hook: Tin cans arrived in 1810. A proper can opener took almost 50 more years.
peek: The tin can was patented in Britain in 1810, but nobody patented a tool to open one until 1858. Early cans were thick and heavy, and the instructions told people to cut them open with a hammer and chisel.
lede: In 1810 an Englishman named Peter Durand patented the idea of keeping food in sealed tin cans. Within a few years a London factory was supplying canned meat to the Royal Navy and to explorers. The cans worked, but getting into them was another matter. A tool made just for opening them was not patented until 1858.

bullets.text: The engineer Bryan Donkin and his partners bought Durand's patent and opened a canning works in Bermondsey, London, around 1812. Their heavy cans were made of iron coated in tin, and the labels advised opening them with a chisel and hammer.

Cans grew thinner and lighter by the 1850s, which finally made a hand tool practical. Ezra Warner of Waterbury, Connecticut, patented a curved blade that was jabbed into the lid and worked around the rim. It was used by soldiers during the American Civil War.

In 1870 William Lyman patented an opener with a rolling wheel that cut around the lid, the basic idea behind most openers today. The version with a toothed wheel to grip the rim came later, in the 1920s.
Even then, plenty of cans needed a tool. Lids that open with a ring pull, with no opener at all, only spread from the 1960s on, more than 150 years after the first can.
